abstract: Traditional metabolic inhibitors have limited clinical efficacy, with issues such as narrow window periods, and compensatory effects. These barriers indicate that effective metabolic therapy requires spatially restricted, temporally coordinated, cell-context-aware, and clinically stratifiable intervention. This review examines how glucose-lactate, lipid-redox, amino acid-immune checkpoint, and nucleotide-adenosine circuits drive tumour progression, immune suppression, and therapeutic escape. We then define the engineering advantages that distinguish nanomedicine from free metabolic drugs, including spatiotemporal control, smart and responsive release, multi-target co-delivery, and organelle targeting. Representative nanomedicine strategies are discussed according to the immunometabolic circuits they modulate, with emphasis on their ability to overcome metabolic compensation, restore immune cell function, and address tumour heterogeneity. Finally, we evaluate key translational challenges, including chemistry, manufacturing and control (CMC), regulatory obstacles, and biomarker selection. This review proposes clinically actionable design principles of nanomedicine for immunometabolic reprogramming.

title: Single-cell study of human ovarian response to phthalate exposure reveals glial cell susceptibility and disruption of adhesion and mitochondrial pathways
abstract: BACKGROUND: Phthalates are known male endocrine disruptors and reproductive toxicants. Despite growing evidence of female effects, mechanistic knowledge in key reproductive organs remains limited, hindering regulations. Here, we conducted an experimental study to map the impact of mono(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (MEHP), the primary metabolite of di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), on adult human ovarian tissue at single-cell resolution. METHODS: Ovarian tissue explants from seven donors (five gender-affirming surgery, two caesarean-section) were exposed to two MEHP concentrations: an epidemiologically relevant 20.51 nM and a 1000-fold higher 20.51 μM. After six days, single-cell RNA sequencing (one donor) and immunostainings (six donors) were used to characterise gene expression changes across cell types. Primary ovarian cells derived from three gender-affirming surgery patients and stem cell-derived Schwann cells were used for validation. FINDINGS: Explants retained all major ovarian cell types, including rare glial cells and oocytes. MEHP altered transcriptomes across all cell types, disrupting pathways related to actin cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Protein analyses confirmed altered EIF5A, MT-ND3, MT-ND4L, and VCL expression, genes linked to mitochondrial translation, OXPHOS, adhesion, and cytoskeleton. MEHP also reduced cell-cell communication, particularly glial-stromal interactions. Mitochondrial stress assay in primary cells indicated increased proton leakage, and Schwann cell responses mirrored the scRNA-seq findings. INTERPRETATION: Ovarian toxicity studies traditionally focus on follicles, but this study reveals the susceptibility of non-follicular cells. Importantly, the sensitivity of ovarian nervous system cells to MEHP offers new mechanistic insights into reported links between phthalates, altered ovarian sensitivity index, and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome. Our findings highlight the need for a holistic assessment of ovarian toxicity that considers all ovarian cell types, not only follicles. FUNDING: Swedish Research Council for Sustainable Development and the European Union.

title: NET-derived DNA is associated with cGAS-STING and type I IFN responses, as supported by monocyte stimulation cultures using plasma from female patients with SLE
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are implicated in type I interferon (IFN) production in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). While NETs are known to activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) via binding to Toll-like receptors, their effects on other immune cells remain underexplored. This study investigated whether NETs in plasma from patients with active SLE trigger cGAS-STING signalling in monocytes and induce the production of type I IFN and other immunomodulatory cytokines. METHODS: Monocytes from healthy donors were cultured with diluted plasma from healthy donors or patients with SLE across varying disease activity, or with in vitro-generated NETs. Activation of the cGAS-STING pathway was assessed by flow cytometric analysis of phosphorylated STING (pSTING) and TBK1 (pTBK1). Cytokine production, including type I IFNs, was quantified using bead-based immunoassays. Only female donor samples meeting the study eligibility criteria were available for inclusion in this cohort. FINDINGS: Plasma MPO-DNA levels correlated with IFNβ levels in patients with SLE (P = 0.002). SLE plasma induced STING and TBK1 phosphorylation, and IFNβ expression in healthy monocytes, with responses increasing according to donor disease activity (P < 0.0005). Experiments with healthy monocytes exposed to in vitro-generated NETs recapitulated these findings, evidenced by increased pSTING and pTBK1 expression and enhanced IFNα and IFNβ secretion (P < 0.05), which were inhibited by cGAS-IN-1. INTERPRETATION: Our findings support a role for NET-associated DNA in activating cGAS-STING signalling and promoting type I IFN production by monocytes in SLE. These findings identify NET-mediated cGAS-STING signalling in monocytes as a pathway that warrants further investigation in the context of type I IFN-driven inflammation in SLE. FUNDING: Not Applicable.

title: A proteome-based classification of paediatric adrenocortical tumours links functional tumour states to clinical outcome and therapeutic vulnerabilities
abstract: BACKGROUND: Paediatric adrenocortical tumours (pACT) are rare endocrine neoplasms characterised by marked biological heterogeneity and variable clinical behaviour. Current risk stratification relies largely on histopathology and clinical staging, which incompletely capture underlying tumour biology. We aimed to define proteome-based subtypes of pACT and evaluate their biological, clinical, and therapeutic relevance. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, we performed mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of 83 pACT and adjacent non-tumour adrenal tissues. Differential abundance analysis, pathway enrichment, consensus clustering, survival analyses, and clinicopathological correlations were performed. A minimal protein classifier was derived using forward feature selection and leave-one-out cross-validation. Cluster-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities were assessed using a curated druggability framework. FINDINGS: Tumours displayed profound proteomic differences compared with adjacent non-tumour adrenal cortex, characterised by activation of cholesterol biosynthesis, steroidogenic, MYC, mTORC1, and cell-cycle programs and suppression of extracellular matrix, adhesion, and immune-related pathways. Unsupervised clustering identified four proteome-defined tumour states that only partially overlapped with histopathological diagnosis. These subtypes differed significantly in endocrine phenotype, vascular invasion, Ki67 index, necrosis, and overall survival (log-rank p = 0.00036). Distinct biological programs included stromal-immune-enriched, mitochondrial steroidogenic, IGF/mTOR-driven anabolic, and highly proliferative chromatin-remodelled states. A five-protein classifier (DAAM2, CIP2A, TSC2, PALS2, and P3H1) reproduced cluster assignments with 92.8% leave-one-out cross-validation accuracy. Cluster-specific analyses identified distinct therapeutic target landscapes, including IGF-axis and epigenetic vulnerabilities. INTERPRETATION: Proteomic profiling defines biologically and clinically distinct pACT subtypes that provide prognostic information beyond histopathology. This framework enables proteome-based stratification, identifies candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities, and can be approximated by a five-protein classifier. FUNDING: German Childhood Cancer Foundation, Mitteldeutsche Kinderkrebsforschung, European Union's EU4Health Programme, Max Planck Society, Onassis Foundation, and Joachim Herz Stiftung.

title: Deciphering the heterogeneity of prodromal α-synucleinopathy: linking brain biotyping and gut dysbiosis in isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder
abstract: BACKGROUND: Isolated/idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a specific prodrome of α-synucleinopathies. We previously identified two distinct clinical-neuroimaging biotypes in iRBD: Biotype 1, marked by widespread cortical-subcortical-cerebellar atrophy with motor and cognitive deficits, and Biotype 2, with preserved brain structure and neurocognition. Converging evidence implicates the gut-brain axis in early α-synucleinopathy, yet its role in these divergent iRBD phenotypes remains unexplored. METHODS: We analysed faecal microbiota using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and structural neuroimaging data from 167 participants (42 Biotype 1, 50 Biotype 2, 75 controls). Microbial features and brain structure were compared across groups. Gut-brain associations were assessed using sparse partial least squares regression to link microbiome features with neuroanatomical patterns. FINDINGS: Overall microbial composition did not significantly differ between Biotype 1 and Biotype 2, and both biotypes showed depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria. Relative to the shared dysbiotic background, Biotype 1 displayed more pronounced taxon- and pathway-level alterations, including enrichment of Collinsella aerofaciens, Cloacibacillus evryensis, and Mogibacterium sp. BX12, which were associated with Biotype 1-specific brain atrophy. Biotype 2 showed milder dysbiosis with fewer differentially abundant species. These patterns were consistent in sensitivity analyses and fully adjusted models. INTERPRETATION: Beyond a shared depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, iRBD biotypes exhibit differences in taxonomic and functional profiles, with these differences being more pronounced in Biotype 1. These findings support a role for the gut-brain axis in early α-synucleinopathy and its phenotypic heterogeneity. FUNDING: This study was funded by the Health and Medical Research Fund of the Food and Health Bureau (Ref No.: 05162876 and 10210686) and Research Grants Council (RGC-CRF Ref No.: C4044-21G) of Hong Kong.

title: The CLEC7A Y238∗ variant and susceptibility to pneumonia: a prospective population-based cohort study and mechanistic investigation
abstract: BACKGROUND: DECTIN-1, a C-type lectin receptor encoded by CLEC7A, mediates antifungal immunity, but its antibacterial role remains unclear. We investigated, using human genetic and animal studies, whether the common loss-of-function CLEC7A Y238∗ variant (rs16910526) influences susceptibility to bacterial respiratory infection, and sought to identify the bacterial ligand mediating DECTIN-1 recognition. METHODS: mice with Streptococcus pneumoniae and non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHi). Affinity proteomics, ELISA, flow cytometry, and NF-κB reporter assays identified and validated the ligand. FINDINGS: Y238∗ carriers had elevated pneumonia risk in adjusted Cox models (HR 1·12, 95% CI 1·04-1·20; p = 0·002; concordant competing-risk sHR 1·12, 1·04-1·20). Clec7a-deficient mice showed gene-dose-dependent impairment of S. pneumoniae clearance, impaired NTHi clearance, and blunted cytokine responses. Affinity pull-down identified elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) as a DECTIN-1 ligand that bound the carbohydrate-recognition domain and activated NF-κB signalling when clustered; orthologues from four bacterial species also bound. INTERPRETATION: These findings support a role for DECTIN-1 in pulmonary antibacterial defence and suggest that inherited deficiency increases pneumonia susceptibility in humans. EF-Tu is a candidate ligand that provides mechanistic support for the association. FUNDING: Swedish Research Council, Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, Swedish Heart Lung Foundation, Swedish Government Funds for Clinical Research (ALF), Skåne County Council's Research and Development Foundation.

title: Immune effects of faecal microbiota transplantation in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a pilot multicentre, randomised, masked, sham-controlled, proof-of concept trial
abstract: Background The gut microbiota modulates peripheral immunity, which is altered in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) may exert immunological effects, but its impact in ALS remains unclear. Methods FETR-ALS was a multicentre, randomised, masked, sham-controlled proof-of-concept trial conducted at four Italian ALS centres. Adults with ALS of 18 months duration or less and forced vital capacity of at least 70% predicted were randomly assigned (2:1) to receive FMT or a sham procedure (SP). The intervention consisted of two nasojejunal administrations of screened-donor faecal suspension at baseline and month 6, without antibiotic preconditioning. The primary endpoint was change in circulating Tregs among CD4 + T cells at 6 months. Secondary endpoints included safety, ALS Functional Rating Scale–Revised slope, respiratory and nutritional measures, survival, and exploratory biomarker profiles. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03766321. Findings Between 2020 and 2024, 43 individuals were screened and 42 were enrolled and randomly assigned to FMT (n = 28; mean age 56.1 years [SD 8.2]; 14 [50%] male) or SP (n = 14; 59.6 years [9.1]; eight [57%] male). Overall, 29 participants completed the second procedure and 6-month follow-up, and Treg measurements were available for 28. The primary outcome was not met: at 6 months, 8/18 (44%) participant receiving FMT versus 2/10 (20%) receiving SP achieved a ≥20% increase in circulating Tregs (odds ratio [OR] 3.20, 95% CI 0.59–25.36; p=0.21). Mean Treg increase was 2.36 percentage points higher with FMT (95% CI 0.19–4.55; p=0.04). ALSFRS-R declined by −1.07 points/month in the SP group and −0.76 points/month in the FMT group, with a between-group difference in monthly decline of 0.31 points/month favouring FMT (95% CI 0.11–0.51; p=0.002). Conversely, at month 6, the MRC score was lower in the FMT group than in the SP group (0.75 versus 0.89; mean difference −0.13, 95% CI –0.26 to 0.00; p=0.042). FMT was associated with 32 adverse events (12.5% severe) versus 14 (28.6% severe) in SP, mostly gastrointestinal or infectious. Interpretation In this exploratory trial, FMT was not associated with major safety concerns. Although the primary endpoint was not met, FMT was associated with a modest increase in circulating Tregs. Funding Italian Ministry of Health.

title: EARLY-ALS: a multicentre study on prodromal amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
abstract: Abstract Neurodegenerative diseases often feature a prolonged presymptomatic phase during which pathological processes evolve before overt clinical manifestation. In Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), defining this prodromal period is critical for identifying early disease features and the optimal window for intervention, yet it remains poorly characterised. In this cross-sectional study, we compared 475 ALS patients with 285 controls recruiting across 20 ALS expert centres in Germany and Switzerland. Participants completed a structured digital questionnaire capturing prodromal complaints, healthcare utilisation, comorbidities, lifestyle factors, and weight changes during the 10 years preceding ALS symptom onset. ALS patients reported substantially higher burden of prodromal complaints than controls (OR=7.50, 95% CI 4.27-13.17; P < 0.001; P adj < 0.001), particularly neuro-motor, sensory, and pain-related symptoms. Prior to symptom onset, ALS patients more frequently consulted neurologists (OR=1.26, CI 1.10-1.44; P < 0.001; P adj = 0.007). Speech therapy consultations were significantly more common among female patients (OR = 2.35, CI 1.05–5.28; P = 0.038) and those with bulbar-onset ALS (OR = 8.67, CI 3.80–19.77; P < 0.001). Prodromal musculoskeletal dysfunction was more frequently reported by ALS patients and exhibited sex- and site-specific patterns. Herniated discs were reported more often by male ALS patients (OR=2.21, CI 1.04-4.68; P = 0.038) and by those with spinal-onset disease (OR=2.32, CI 1.38-3.93; P = 0.002). ALS patients more often completed lower secondary education (OR=1.93, CI 1.24-3.01; P = 0.004; P adj = 0.020) and were more likely to have worked in physically demanding occupations (OR=2.21, CI 1.42-3.43; P < 0.001; P adj = 0.003). Lifestyle factors differed significantly, with higher prior consumption of caffeine (OR=7.21, CI 3.27–15.89; P < 0.001; P adj < 0.001), alcohol (OR=2.25, CI 1.47–3.43; P < 0.001; P adj = 0.002), and cigarettes (OR=1.64, CI 1.20–2.24; P = 0.002) among ALS patients ( P adj = 0.011). Weight trajectories differed by sex ( P = 0.009), with male ALS patients showing significant loss already during the pre-onset phase ( P < 0.001). These findings demonstrate that ALS is preceded by a distinct prodromal phase characterised by mild motor impairment, altered healthcare engagement, and sex- and site-specific patterns in comorbidities, lifestyle, and metabolic change. Characterising these early features of ALS may facilitate earlier diagnosis and enable timely enrolment in clinical trials.

title: The time has come: integrating vaccination and vector control for Aedes-borne disease prevention
abstract: Dengue control has entered a new phase. Vaccination and vector control are often considered separate interventions, yet they act at different and potentially complementary points in the transmission cycle. Vaccination provides individual-level protection against dengue in eligible populations, whereas vector control reduces mosquito abundance, vector competence, or transmission potential, thereby reducing population-level exposure. The key question is therefore not whether either approach has value in isolation, but how vaccination, biological vector control, and evidence-based routine vector-control measures can be combined within integrated prevention programs.

title: Sustained type I interferon activity and N-antigenemia form a vicious cycle during severe COVID-19
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although antigenemia is associated with poor outcomes in respiratory viral infections, the underlying mechanisms driving viral bloodstream dissemination remain not fully understood. Herein, we aimed to characterise SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N)-antigenemia kinetics in patients with severe COVID-19. We also sought to identify host and viral determinants associated with viral dissemination through a multiparametric integrated analysis and assess the associated risk of death. METHODS: This observational study included hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 across three independent cohorts (discovery, n = 66; confirmation, n = 137; validation, n = 27), used respectively for identification, replication, and validation of findings, along with patients with mild COVID-19 and with severe influenza infection, as a disease severity and non-COVID-19 control group. From blood and nasal samples, N-antigenemia levels were analysed in relation to 45 host/viral parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association with in-hospital mortality. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify host determinants, and in vitro primary human airway epithelial models were used to assess epithelial barrier integrity and viral translocation. FINDINGS: Across cohorts, we observed a significantly higher detection rate and concentration of N-antigenemia in patients with severe COVID-19 at admission compared to those with mild COVID-19 or controls (fold change [FC] >54.7, p < 0.001 [Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post-hoc]). Type-I interferon (IFN-I) activity was the strongest correlate of N-antigenemia (ρ = 0.72, p.adj < 0.001 [Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg]), and longitudinal analyses revealed a strong positive sigmoidal relationship (p < 0.001 [approximate Wald test]). Patients with severe COVID-19 with neutralising autoantibodies against IFN-I lacked detectable N-antigenemia, further supporting a link between systemic viral dissemination and IFN-I activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed higher expression of interferon-stimulated genes in monocytes and dendritic cells in patients with a high N-antigenemia level. Furthermore, high N-antigenemia at hospital admission was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.0-6.7; p = 0.042 [Wald test]). Finally, we demonstrated that prolonged IFN-I exposure in vitro appears to impair epithelial barrier integrity. INTERPRETATION: These findings suggest that sustained IFN-I activity is associated with systemic viral dissemination and epithelial barrier dysfunction in patient with severe COVID-19. The concordance between clinical observations and in vitro data supports a potential link between prolonged IFN-I responses and these processes, although causality remains to be established. These results highlight the potential importance of the timing and duration of IFN-I immunity and warrant further investigation of its clinical relevance. FUNDING: Agence Nationale de Recherches sur le Sida et les Hépatites Virales (ANRS), ANRS Maladies Infectieuses Émergentes (ANRS MIE), Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR), Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale (INSERM), European Union Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme, CAPNET, and Klinbeforsk.

title: Converging arboviral outbreaks demand disease-agnostic public health responses
abstract: The scale of the 2023–25 Oropouche virus (OROV) outbreak in Brazil was itself unprecedented, and coincided with a record-breaking 2023–24 dengue epidemic, presenting challenges in diagnosing and tracking both. In name and perception, arthropod-borne virus (arbovirus) outbreaks are often considered separate and distinct, yet nature never neatly compartmentalises, and the same meteorological and ecological factors that drive one can affect many. Expanding insect-vector habitats increasingly allows arboviruses to stably co-circulate in overlapping regions.

title: Molecular mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of triiodothyroacetic acid (Triac) in patients with resistance to thyroid hormone β (RTHβ): a multicentre, international, retrospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Disease features in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ), caused by THRB mutations, arise from insensitivity to thyroid hormone in tissues expressing thyroid hormone receptor (TR)β and from lifelong thyrotoxic effects in TRα1-expressing tissues, posing substantial cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. The T3-analogue triiodothyroacetic acid (Triac) holds potential as an effective treatment. Systematic data on Triac therapy in RTHβ are lacking, and the mechanisms through which Triac acts are unclear. This study aims to elucidate these knowledge gaps. METHODS: Clinical and biochemical data were obtained through an, international retrospective cohort study in patients with RTHβ. Transcriptional activity of all TRβ mutants, on the background of the pituitary-expressed β2 receptor isoform and positively (DR+4-TRE) or negatively (TSHα-TRE) regulated reporter genes plus T3 or Triac, was studied. Thyroid function and TSH responses to T3 and Triac were tested in zebrafish expressing TRβ mutants. FINDINGS: We collected data from 28 patients with RTHβ (range: 0.4-73.1 years) with 18 unique mutations treated with Triac in 6 centres. Triac reduced TSH (by 43%) and FT4 (by 37%) concentrations in all heterozygous patients, supported by consistent findings in zebrafish. Our functional studies showed that TRβ2 mutants exhibited reduced (all) or absent (G432del) T3-dependent transcriptional activity, with similar EC50 and IC50 values for T3 and Triac, except for R316H, which showed a 5-times lower EC50/IC50 value for Triac compared to T3. INTERPRETATION: In this international, multicentre study we have documented that Triac lowers elevated FT4 concentrations in patients with RTHβ effectively. Integrating our clinical and molecular observations we suggest that Triac can act via different modes of action, with activation of the wild-type receptor being a relevant mechanism. Our study may inform clinical management and could shape future interventional studies in patients with RTHβ. FUNDING: Financial support is acknowledged by WL (Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University) WEV (ZonMw (Dutch Research Council, VIDI 09150172210071)), KC (Wellcome (210755/Z/18/Z), NIHR Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre (NIHR20312) and Medical Research Council United Kingdom (MRC_MU_UU_00014/40)), LP (European Union - Next Generation EU - NRRP M6C2 - Investment 2.1 Enhancement and strengthening of biomedical research in the NHS (code: PNRR-MR1-2022-12375726).

title: Exploration of the genetic architecture of ANCA-associated vasculitis
abstract: Background Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a complex autoimmune disease with distinct clinical and serological subtypes. Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several susceptibility loci, particularly within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), but the broader genetic architecture and causal variants underlying AAV remain incompletely defined. Methods We conducted a genome-wide association study including 2068 individuals with AAV and 3258 controls of European ancestry. The discovery cohort comprised a previously published GWAS dataset supplemented with newly recruited cases. Analyses were stratified by clinical (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA] and microscopic polyangiitis [MPA]) and serological (proteinase 3–ANCA [PR3] and myeloperoxidase–ANCA [MPO]) subtypes. Findings were evaluated in an independent case cohort of 465 individuals. We performed conditional and joint analyses of the HLA region, functional fine-mapping, linkage disequilibrium score regression, and integrative multi-omics analyses to prioritise candidate causal variants and assess genetic correlations. Findings We identified eight previously unreported loci and replicated four known loci associated with AAV at genome-wide significance. Within the HLA region, HLA-DPB1∗04 showed the strongest association with AAV, GPA, and PR3 subtypes, whereas HLA-DRB1∗04 was most strongly associated with MPO and MPA. Conditional analyses identified additional independent effects, including amino acid variation in HLA-DQA1 . SNP-based heritability estimates indicated a substantial genetic contribution to AAV (h 2 = 0·40). Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared heritability with multiple traits, including celiac disease and hypothyroidism. Integrative analyses highlighted candidate genes, including HCG9 and PRTN3 , and implicated protein interaction networks involving genes related to neutrophil biology. Protein–protein interaction analysis identified networks involving genes implicated in AAV risk, including PRTN3 , AZU1 , ELANE , and SERPINA1 . Interpretation These findings expand the genetic landscape of AAV and support a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture involving both MHC and non-MHC loci. The integration of genetic association, functional annotation, and network analyses suggests that disease susceptibility is mediated through multiple biological pathways, including immune regulation and neutrophil function. These insights may inform future mechanistic studies, improved disease stratification, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. Funding National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

title: CNPY3 variants associated with a recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy affect inflammasome and TLR function
abstract: BACKGROUND: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. METHODS: 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. FINDINGS: Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. INTERPRETATION: CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. FUNDING: Interdisciplinary Center of Clinical Research and Jena School of Molecular Medicine, Jena University Hospital; Friedrich Schiller University Jena; The Wellcome Trust; The Medical Research Council; The MSA Trust; The National Institute for Health Research University College London Hospitals Biomedical Research Centre; The Michael J Fox Foundation; Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council; The Fidelity Trust; Rosetrees Trust; Ataxia UK; Brain Research UK; Sparks GOSH Charity; Alzheimer's Research UK; CureDRPLA; UK Dementia Research Institute; Parkinson's UK; South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, Norway; France Genomic Medicine Plan 2025; Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft; European Commission; Federal Government of Germany; State of Thuringia; Pakistan Science Foundation; King Abdullah International Medical Research Center; Science and Technology Development Fund; King Salman Center for Disability Research.

title: Early detection of immunoglobulin A against a vaccine backbone protein enables fast, durable, and objective identification of individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus
abstract: BACKGROUND: rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine is recommended for prevention of Ebola virus (EBOV) infection and disease (EVD). However, breakthrough EBOV infections have been observed in vaccinees. Currently available diagnostic and research assays cannot reliably distinguish individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus from those previously infected with the virus. This limitation complicates interpretation of vaccine-effectiveness studies, seroepidemiologic investigations, and estimates of infection or attack rates. The ability to differentiate vaccine-induced immune responses from those resulting from natural infection remains an important unmet public health and research need. METHODS: We developed a multiplex sero-diagnostic assay simultaneously detecting IgA, IgG, and IgM antibodies against vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus nucleoprotein (VSV-N), a vaccine-specific marker absent in natural infection, and EBOV-GP, the vaccine's target antigen. We evaluated longitudinal samples from 30 individuals after vaccination and 30 placebo (saline) recipients, as well as 8 participants from a long-term vaccination follow-up study. FINDINGS: We detected increase in all antibodies against both protein antigens in vaccinated individuals. Critically, the assay reveals that anti-VSV-N IgA responses emerge earlier and more robustly than anti-GP responses in vaccinees, establishing anti-N IgA as a definitive, early, and durable biomarker of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity. INTERPRETATION: The assay enables rapid, accurate identification of vaccine recipients and supports real-time assessment of vaccine effectiveness during outbreaks. Furthermore, the assay's adaptability to the expanding pipeline of VSV-vectored vaccines positions it as a transformative diagnostic platform for accelerating preparedness for future infectious disease threats and outbreak response strategies. FUNDING: Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the Divisions of Intramural Research (DIR) and Clinical Research (DCR) of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH).

title: Decreased function of fatty acid desaturase 1 is associated with placental foetal vascular malperfusion and highlights the key role of the maternal–foetal interface
abstract: BACKGROUND: Placental foetal vascular malperfusion (PFVM) is a chronic disorder characterised by impaired blood flow and abnormal vascular development, inducing adverse neonatal outcomes. Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) play a crucial role in placenta health. We aimed to explore the role of genetic variation in LC-PUFA metabolism in PFVM risk as well as underlying mechanisms. METHODS: Associations were examined between two functional polymorphisms (rs174538 and rs174556) of the fatty acid desaturase 1 (FADS1) gene encoding the rate-limiting enzyme for LC-PUFA metabolism and PFVM among pregnant women (n = 646). Placental transcriptomes were correlated with PFVM and FADS1 genotypes. Various assays were performed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells and trophoblasts with FADS1 inhibitor and LC-PUFA interventions to characterise their function changes. FINDINGS: Low-function alleles of both polymorphisms were significantly associated with increased PFVM risk and decreased placental FADS1 transcription level. In placenta tissue, lower FADS1 expression is also associated with PFVM. PFVM-associated genes are enriched to pathways related to immune responses, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, which overlap with the genes and pathways associated with the risk alleles and demonstrate a cell-type enrichment to endothelial cells. In vitro, FADS1 inhibition impairs multiple functions of and interactions between endothelial and trophoblast cells. These impairments are reversed by LC-PUFA supplementation. INTERPRETATION: These findings highlight the impact of maternal LC-PUFA homoeostasis in placenta health and suggest that maternal FADS1 variants can potentially be an early diagnostic marker for PFVM. Our data supports PUFA metabolism as a precision therapeutic or preventive target to reduce placental dysfunction risk. FUNDING: NIH, Wayne State University and Michigan State University.

title: Relationship extraction for adverse drug events in clinical notes using large language models: a retrospective cross-sectional study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes. METHODS: We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models. FINDINGS: Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings. INTERPRETATION: This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety. FUNDING: None.

title: Genetically informed therapy for valvular heart disease: what, where, and when to target
abstract: Treatment of valvular heart disease (VHD) has advanced substantially through surgical and transcatheter valve repair and replacement. However, effective pharmacological therapies that directly modify valve pathobiology remain lacking for most forms of VHD.1 In this issue of eBioMedicine, Moura-Ferreira et al.2 bring genetics and therapeutics together by linking VHD-associated variation to target tractability, existing drugs, and clinical and experimental evidence. Among 431 candidate genes with available tractability information, only 51 were linked to existing compounds, corresponding to 388 pharmacological agents.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and neurodegeneration biomarkers in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multicohort observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS. METHODS: We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153). FINDINGS: Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]). INTERPRETATION: Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS. FUNDING: This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). A complete list of funding organisations is provided in Acknowledgements.

title: Adenomyosis and association between ultrasonographic features and pregnancy outcomes in women with infertility or pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adenomyosis has been shown to reduce live birth rates and increase the risk of pregnancy loss. The diagnosis is often established by ultrasonographic assessment using the revised Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) criteria. However, the reproductive impact of specific sonographic features remains unclear. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to investigate whether individual ultrasonographic adenomyosis features influence pregnancy outcomes in women with infertility or pregnancy loss. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar (most recent 200 records) from inception to May 11th, 2026. Observational and interventional studies reporting specific ultrasonographic features of adenomyosis in women with infertility and/or pregnancy loss were included. Primary outcomes were clinical pregnancy, live birth, and pregnancy loss. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, as appropriate by study design. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models, with common-effects models applied where appropriate; remaining evidence was synthesised narratively. Certainty of evidence was assessed by GRADE. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251077005). FINDINGS: = 0%). Narrative synthesis suggested poorer reproductive outcomes with adenomyosis features located near the endometrium and with larger uterine volume. The overall certainty was low or very low for 20 out of 21 outcomes, and moderate for one, primarily driven by imprecision and indirectness related to variation in diagnostic criteria across studies. INTERPRETATION: Reproductive outcomes in adenomyosis vary according to specific ultrasonographic features, supporting feature-based reporting beyond a binary diagnosis. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent ultrasonographic diagnostic criteria, variable application of MUSA definitions, and differences in fertility treatment protocols, warrants cautious interpretation of pooled estimates. Standardised definitions and reporting of adenomyosis features are needed to improve evidence synthesis and clinical translation. FUNDING: The Novo Nordisk Foundation and the Danish Research Council.

title: Immunogenicity and protective efficacy of single-dose adenoviral vaccines expressing Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus GP38, Gc, or nucleoprotein antigens in mice: a preclinical study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a highly pathogenic, tick-borne orthonairovirus responsible for severe human disease, yet no approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. The glycoprotein precursor (GPC), including its GP38, Gn, and Gc components, and the nucleoprotein (NP) have been explored as vaccine targets with varying success. A chimpanzee adenoviral vector (ChAdOx) vaccine encoding full-length GPC previously conferred complete protection in mice, supporting Phase I evaluation. However, the essential protective components and mechanisms of vaccine-induced immunity remain unclear. METHODS: We evaluated ChAdOx2 vaccines encoding individual GPC subunits (GP38, Gn, or Gc), full-length GPC, or NP in a lethal interferon receptor-deficient mouse model. Protective efficacy and immune responses were assessed to define protective immunogens and mechanisms. FINDINGS: Single-dose vaccination with ChAdOx2-GP38 or ChAdOx2-Gc conferred complete survival (6/6 per group; both p = 0.0005 vs PBS), with minimal histopathology and viral RNA burden at the 21-day study endpoint, comparable to full-length GPC (6/6; p = 0.0005 vs PBS). ChAdOx2-NP likewise conferred complete survival (6/6; p = 0.0008 vs PBS) and elicited robust NP-specific immune responses. In contrast, ChAdOx2-Gn conferred partial survival (2/6; p = 0.0101 vs PBS), while low-dose GPC vaccination provided limited protection (1/6; p = 0.0617 vs PBS) with impaired IgG responses while preserving T-cell responses. Immunological analyses showed that GP38, Gc, and full-length GPC constructs induced robust antibody responses with similar Fcγ receptor engagement and limited neutralising activity. INTERPRETATION: These findings identify GP38 and Gc as individually protective immunogens while reinforcing GPC and NP as effective vaccine targets. Together, these data support roles for non-neutralising antibodies and T-cell responses in protection against CCHFV and continued development of ChAdOx-vectored vaccines for clinical use. FUNDING: This research was supported by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

title: Early treatment with tecovirimat against mpox disease in cynomolgus macaques
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tecovirimat was developed as an antiviral countermeasure against orthopoxviruses and approved by the US Food and Drug Administration Animal Rule based on efficacy in preclinical studies and clinical pharmacokinetic and safety trials. However, recent randomised clinical trials in patients with mpox who initiated tecovirimat an average of 6-9 days after onset of symptoms did not show improvement in time to resolution of skin lesions. Here, we evaluated whether timing of tecovirimat initiation influenced antiviral efficacy following mpox infection in nonhuman primates and defined the therapeutic window for treatment initiation. METHODS: mpox clade IIb virus. Oral tecovirimat (10 mg/kg, once daily for 14 days) treatment was initiated on Day 2 (post-exposure and pre-symptomatic), Day 5 (early symptomatic), or Day 9 (peak symptomatic) after mpox challenge, or no treatment was given as a control group. The primary study endpoint was area under the curve (AUC) and peak numbers of progressive skin lesions. The secondary endpoint was AUC and peak levels of plasma viral loads. Additional analyses included total skin lesions, adaptive immune responses, and transcriptomic signatures. FINDINGS: Treatment adherence was 100%. All tecovirimat-treated animals survived to study completion on Day 28, whereas two untreated control animals required early euthanisation on Days 16 and 17. Tecovirimat efficacy was time-dependent. Progressive skin lesion AUC was significantly lower when treatment was initiated on Day 2 (P < 0.0001) or Day 5 (P = 0.0359) compared with untreated controls, but treatment was largely ineffective when initiated on Day 9 (P > 0.99). INTERPRETATION: In this randomised preclinical study, tecovirimat demonstrated antiviral therapeutic efficacy but only when initiated early prior to peak viraemia. These findings emphasise the importance of early initiation of treatment and define the therapeutic window for optimal tecovirimat treatment in nonhuman primates. FUNDING: This study was supported by SIGA Technologies.

title: Predictors of HIV reservoir size and decay dynamics in early-treated paediatric infection: a prospective, multicentre longitudinal cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Early antiretroviral therapy (ART) after perinatal HIV infection can restrict reservoir size and diversity, offering potential for remission. We evaluated HIV-1 DNA dynamics up to four years of age and predictors of reservoir size in early-treated African children. METHODS: copies/million PBMC) and longitudinal HIV-1 DNA decay. Multivariable models were developed to identify predictors of reservoir size using generalised additive regression models, and decay dynamics were evaluated using mixed-effects Poisson models including random intercepts and viral load slopes. FINDINGS: Of 207 children, 155 (75%) had >12 months of follow-up. HIV was diagnosed at a median age of 31 days (IQR: 0, 47) and ART started at 33 days (IQR: 23.5, 69.5). Nineteen of 155 (12.3%) had undetectable HIV-1 DNA at year 4. Median decay rate was -0.020 log10 copies/million cells/month (-0.212/year). Smaller reservoirs at year 3 were associated with lower pre-ART viral load (β = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.09, 0.43) and faster first-year HIV-1 DNA decay rate (β = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.02, 2.19), with trends toward smaller reservoirs among females (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.87, 0.04) and larger reservoirs among children whose mothers reported social challenges (β = 0.42, 95% CI: -0.04, 0.87). Faster decay correlated with longer time on ART, lower serial viral loads, sustained viral suppression >12 months, earlier ART initiation, and region (Mali). Maternal health issues correlated with slower decay. Eleven "excellent controllers" maintained durable viral suppression, immunological control, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA at last follow-up. INTERPRETATION: Early virological parameters may help identify children likely to develop smaller HIV reservoirs. Early ART is key to faster reservoir reduction. Maternal health issues influence reservoir decay, reflecting a parental legacy effect. Sex differences should be further explored to understand mechanisms of reservoir control. Children with sustained virological suppression, preserved immune status, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA may represent candidates with favourable characteristics for HIV remission strategies, as these factors have been associated with a reduced burden of persistent HIV infection and have been observed in rare cases of post-treatment control. FUNDING: EPIICAL consortium through ViiV Healthcare and Penta Foundation.

title: Cataract genetics: bringing disease modification into focus
abstract: Cataract surgery is among the most effective interventions in ophthalmology, yet it treats the consequence of lens opacification rather than the biological processes that give rise to it.1,2 For visually significant cataract, surgery remains the definitive treatment, and no pharmacological therapy has been established to eliminate existing opacity or reliably slow its progression.2 As populations age, the burden of cataract and demand for surgical care will continue to grow, while access to timely, high-quality surgery remains markedly unequal worldwide.

title: Infant gut microbiome neuroactive pathways link to social disadvantage, toddler neurodevelopment, cognitive and behavioural outcomes: a longitudinal cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Early life is a critical window for co-development of the brain and gut microbiome (GM). Evidence supports a role for the GM in brain development, but longitudinal human data remain limited, particularly regarding the influence of social disadvantage (SD), a powerful determinant of child mental health and neurodevelopment. Here, we examine longitudinal relationships between the GM and neurodevelopmental outcomes over the first three years of life, and the impact of SD on them. METHODS: We sequenced and analysed stool samples of 187 children, collected at 5 timepoints over 4-36 months of life (MOL; 905 samples) using a whole-metagenome sequencing approach. Associations between GM-derived Gut-Brain Modules (GBM) and neuroactive potential were assessed using generalised linear mixed models, adjusting for covariates. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated by Bayley-III (cognitive, language, and motor), and neurobehavioural dysregulation and externalising/internalising-behaviour by the Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (ITSEA) and Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA). FINDINGS: Temporal changes were observed in GBMs, including glutamate/GABA synthesis and degradation pathways, as well as short-chain fatty acids. GM community structure and GBMs were significantly associated with concurrent and later Bayley-III outcomes, most consistently for cognition and language (FDR < 0.10). Several GBMs were associated with both neurobehavioural outcomes and SD, including S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) synthesis, butyrate synthesis, and glutamate and GABA synthesis II (FDR < 0.10). A partial mediating effect between SD and 36 MOL language outcomes was observed using SAM synthesis at 4 MOL (β = -0.042, P = 0.048). INTERPRETATION: This longitudinal cohort study of GM neuroactive metabolic capacity across early transitional developmental windows reveals a dynamic pattern of GM-derived neuroactive metabolic pathways and identifies specific pathways associated with later neurodevelopmental (cognitive, language) and neurobehavioural outcomes, even after controlling for important covariates. These pathways are shaped by the socioeconomic status of mothers, starting with in-utero exposure, and GBMs partially mediated this effect. The study identifies microbial pathways associated with both SD and neurodevelopmental outcomes, highlighting potential biological processes that may contribute to neurodevelopmental risk and warrant further investigation. FUNDING: This work was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, March of Dimes, Children's Discovery Institute, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, and National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences.

title: Prognostic value of microRNA expression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) ranks among the deadliest malignancies, with limited survival benefits despite recent therapeutic advances. Few prognostic biomarkers are available for PDAC monitoring in clinical practice. We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate and synthesise evidence on the prognostic significance of miRNA expression in PDAC. Methods The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023463542). We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, CENTRAL, and Embase on January 27, 2026, to identify studies assessing miRNA expression levels in patients with PDAC with reported overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS) outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Prediction intervals (PI) were reported if feasible. Separate analyses were performed by miRNA functional categories: oncogenic, tumour suppressor, chemoresistance-related, metastasis-related, and dual-role miRNAs. Findings A total of 142 studies, including 13,824 patients, were included. High expression of oncogenic miRNAs was associated with worse univariate OS (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.38–2.10; 95% PI 0.63–4.57) and PFS (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.63–3.10; 95% PI 1.11–4.55). High expression of chemoresistance-related miRNAs was associated with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.68–2.66; 95% PI 0.96–4.68) and PFS (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.89–3.33; 95% PI 1.58–3.97). Between-study heterogeneity varied substantially across pooled analyses (I 2 range 0–94%). miRNA-21 was the most frequently studied individual biomarker and showed a consistent association with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.95–2.57; 95% PI 1.92–2.61). Interpretation Elevated expression of oncogenic and chemoresistance-related miRNAs is associated with worse survival outcomes in PDAC. However, substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals observed in several pooled analyses indicate variability in effect sizes across studies. Among the investigated biomarkers, miRNA-21 has shown the most consistent prognostic association and may represent the strongest candidate for future clinical implementation. Further validation and standardisation are required before miRNA profiling can be integrated into routine clinical practice. Funding None to declare.

title: Mapping human genetic associations to drug targets in valvular heart disease: an integrative evidence synthesis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Valvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum. METHODS: We retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741). FINDINGS: We identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability. INTERPRETATION: This genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies. FUNDING: Limburg Clinical Research Centre of UHasselt, Jessa and ZOL; British Heart Foundation; National Institute for Health and Care Research; UK Research and Innovation; European Research Council; Horizon Europe.

title: Lipid dynamics and cardiovascular risk profiles on carbohydrate- or saturated fat-based diets: secondary analysis of the CARBFUNC trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity involves complex changes in energy metabolism and increased cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk independently of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). Diets high or low in carbohydrates or fats can be effective for reversing obesity, but their distinct effects on metabolic health and detailed lipid profiles may differentially impact overall CVD risk, particularly with large differences in saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake. METHODS: In a 2-year randomised controlled trial, 193 males and females with obesity were assigned to 1) an acellular carbohydrate-based diet (A-HCLF, comparator arm), 2) a cellular carbohydrate-based diet (C-HCLF), or 3) a low-carbohydrate high-fat (LCHF) diet (75 energy percent fat, thereof 30 SFAs). As secondary outcomes of the trial, plasma lipids and lipoprotein particle subfractions were quantified by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy assay, and coronary artery calcium score by CT imaging. Data were analysed by constrained linear mixed-effects modelling. FINDINGS: Attrition was 74 (39%), 114 (59%), 128 (67%), 135 (70%), and 162 (84%) at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 24 months, respectively. Self-reported adherence ranged from 63 to 85% up to 12 months and 40-60% for the last 12 months. During the first 9-12 months, the LCHF group showed significantly greater reductions than the A-HCLF comparator and C-HCLF diets in very low-density lipoprotein particles (VLDLs), triacylglycerols (TAGs), remnant cholesterol, and the TAG/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) ratio, alongside increases in HDL-C, total apolipoprotein A1 (apoA1), apoA1 in large HDL particles, LDL-C (attributed to large LDL particles), and the LDL-C/apolipoprotein B ratio. At 24 months, there were still greater reductions on the LCHF compared to the A-HCLF diet for TAGs, VLDL particles, remnant cholesterol, and the TAG/HDL-C ratio, as well as a greater increase in large LDL particles. INTERPRETATION: In adults with obesity, an LCHF diet rich in SFA markedly lowered TAG-rich remnants and raised HDL-C and apoA1 compared to higher-carbohydrate diets, while shifting LDL toward larger particles without significantly increasing apoB or small LDLs-a pattern that may indicate greater lipid turnover. FUNDING: This work was supported by the Trond Mohn Research Foundation, Bergen (Norway), the University of Bergen (Norway), Kostfonden, Stockholm (Sweden), and the Norwegian Health Association.

title: Alcohol disrupts spatial coordination of autophagy–lysosome pathways to impair intestinal barrier integrity
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) drives intestinal barrier dysfunction, endotoxemia, and liver injury, yet the epithelial mechanisms remain undefined. Autophagy and lysosomes maintain intestinal epithelial homoeostasis and barrier integrity, but their response to chronic alcohol exposure is unclear. METHODS: Human intestinal tissues from individuals with and without AUD were analysed alongside human intestinal organoids. Wild-type, CAG-RFP-EGFP-LC3, GFP-LC3B, and Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice underwent chronic-binge ethanol feeding. Organoids and Caco-2 cells were exposed to ethanol (50 mM) with or without bafilomycin A1 or Torin-2. Autophagy-lysosome pathways were assessed using transcriptomics, immunofluorescence, biochemical fractionation, and flux reporters. FINDINGS: Alcohol induced heterogeneous autophagy-lysosome responses characterised by lysosomal stress/adaptive remodelling. These changes occurred with limited autophagosome formation and maturation, resulting in impaired autophagic throughput. These responses differed along the crypt-villus axis and between intestinal regions. Disrupted autophagy was associated with altered trafficking and accumulation of claudin-2. Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice exhibited increased baseline intestinal permeability vs wild-type controls (p = 0.03). Following ethanol exposure, Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice showed greater intestinal permeability (p = 0.003), circulating and hepatic endotoxin (p = 0.002), hepatic triglycerides (p = 0.01), and serum ALT (p = 0.02) vs ethanol-fed wild-type mice. INTERPRETATION: Alcohol disrupts intestinal autophagy-lysosome homoeostasis in a spatially heterogeneous manner, accompanied by defective epithelial proteostasis and tight junction dysregulation. Impaired autophagosome formation exacerbates gut permeability and liver injury, supporting intestinal autophagy as a potential therapeutic target in alcohol-associated disease. Broader applicability of the human findings requires validation in larger cohorts. FUNDING: This study was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera
abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. METHODS: Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. FINDINGS: Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. INTERPRETATION: Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. FUNDING: Defense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

title: Associations between salivary HHV-6 and long COVID severity in a cross-sectional, case–control analysis
abstract: Background Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Methods Our cross-sectional, case–control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Findings Detection of salivary EBV and HHV-6 DNA copies was highest early in the morning. There were no significant differences in salivary cortisol, testosterone, or oestradiol, or in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the LC and control groups. However, salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated LC propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI=0.02–0.44, p=0.015, adj. p=0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI=0.02–1.36, p=0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI=0.05–0.42, p=0.013) scores. Interpretation The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. While we did not identify a relationship between salivary EBV DNA and LC, EBV may still play a role at earlier time points in the disease course, or in compartments not sampled in this study. These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in LC pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in LC. Funding This work was supported in part by the Else Kröner Fresenius Prize for Medical Research 2023 (to AI), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute Collaborative COVID-19 Initiative (to AI), and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (to AI), the Polybio Research Foundation (to AI and DP) and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation (to DP). National Institutes for Health (NIH) funding sources supported AT, SB and CM.

title: Characterising the genomic landscape of two clinical risk groups in CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders with cutaneous involvement: a multi-institutional retrospective study
abstract: BACKGROUND: CD30+ T cell lymphoproliferative disorders (CD30+ T LPD) with cutaneous involvement comprise a diverse group of neoplasms with variable clinical outcomes. The molecular mechanisms underlying the prognostic differences in these diseases are poorly understood. METHODS: In this multi-institutional retrospective study, 79 patients with CD30+ T LPD were evaluated. DNA and RNA sequencing were performed on skin biopsy samples to characterise molecular features. Patients were assigned to low- and high-risk groups based on treatment recommendations in clinical records. Pathogenic pathways, immune microenvironments, transcriptomic profiles, driver mutations, and mutation signatures were compared between the risk groups. FINDINGS: Across risk groups, there was high mutational recurrence in genes involved in epigenetic regulation and intracellular signalling pathways. Mutational signature analysis revealed a shared prevalence of 5-methylcytosine deamination, UV exposure, defective mismatch repair, and POLE-associated proofreading deficiency. In contrast, gene set enrichment analysis showed that the high-risk group was enriched in pathways governing cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and immune activation compared to the low-risk group. Furthermore, immune microenvironment deconvolution showed a higher abundance of resting dendritic cells in the low-risk group. Finally, high-risk patients exhibited significant overexpression of clinically relevant proteins, highlighting potential alternative treatment approaches for this population. INTERPRETATION: Mutation analyses suggest diverse pathogenesis in these diseases. The high-risk and low-risk groups diverge in gene expression profiles and immune microenvironment, suggesting that these biological differences hold prognostic significance. Molecularly informed therapeutic strategies should be investigated prospectively through clinical trials. FUNDING: This work was supported by developmental funds of the Duke Cancer Institute as part of the P30 Cancer Center Support Grant. Data generation was supported in an unrestricted fashion by the NIH, Data Driven Bioscience, Amazon and Google. SSD was supported by the Wellcome Trust Foundation and the NIH.

title: Advances in the management of pneumonia caused by drug-resistant bacteria: from antimicrobial optimisation to integrated treatment adaptation
abstract: Management of drug-resistant bacterial pneumonia has become increasingly precise, but early precision does not remove the need to reinterpret the patient's course during illness. Active and appropriate empirical therapy, informed by local epidemiology, remains essential, yet treatment often begins before the definitive microbiological profile is available or adequate drug exposure can be confirmed. While rapid diagnostics and pharmacological optimisation can narrow this initial uncertainty, the harder problem arises when antimicrobial treatment appears plausible but the patient shows delayed improvement, clinical deterioration, or incomplete recovery. These trajectories should not be treated as a single form of antibiotic failure. Instead, they require reassessment of whether the dominant limitation is persistent infection, inadequate drug exposure, dysregulated host response, a non-infectious mimic, or repair-limited recovery. In this Review, we propose a trajectory-guided conceptual framework that links management to the process most likely to limit recovery and distinguishes clinically implementable interventions from emerging translational concepts.

title: Serum neurofilament light chain and the 2024 McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2024 McDonald criteria broaden the definition of multiple sclerosis (MS), enabling diagnosis in individuals with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria. We assessed whether these criteria identify such cases using independent laboratory/imaging biomarkers and whether these biomarkers predict subsequent disease activity. METHODS: Participants with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria were included and stratified according to the 2024 criteria. Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) and 3T brain MRI measures-including normalised brain volumes, T2 lesion load (T2LL), cortical lesion (CL) and paramagnetic rim lesion (PRL)-were compared between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2024-negative groups, and with age/sex matched McDonald2017-positive cases according to the 2017 criteria; predictors of disease activity were assessed using penalised-Cox regression. FINDINGS: A total of 141 participants were included: 95 not meeting the 2017 criteria (n = 64 asymptomatic MRI findings; n = 31 clinical presentations), stratified as McDonald2024-positive (n = 46) or McDonald2024-negative (n = 49), and 46 McDonald2017-positive cases. McDonald2024-positive vs. McDonald2024-negative cases showed higher age-corrected sNfL Z-scores (median 0.28[IQR 0.76] vs. -0.12[0.82], p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), reduced normalised thalamic volume (mean 0.009±[SD]0.0007 vs. 0.010 ± 0.0007, p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), and higher CL (1[4] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR < 0.001) and PRL (1[1] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR = 0.003) counts (differences remaining significant after age/sex, disease duration and T2LL adjustments). Biomarker profiles were comparable between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2017-positive cases. Penalised-Cox regression (n = 52) identified sNfL Z-score and PRL presence as the most consistently selected predictors of disease activity, with higher bootstrap stability for sNfL (0.84) than PRL (0.76), and good model discrimination (C-index = 0.71). INTERPRETATION: The 2024 McDonald criteria identify individuals not meeting the 2017 criteria who already exhibit MS-like neuroinflammatory/neurodegenerative pathological changes. These are reflected by laboratory and imaging biomarkers, including sNfL, which may predict subsequent disease activity and complement current diagnostic frameworks to support early clinical decision-making. FUNDING: King Baudouin Foundation; Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc; Fondation Charcot Stichting; Fund for Scientific Research (FNRS); ECTRIMS; Biogen; Sanofi.

title: Identification of peptide epitopes in major antigens of Yersinia pestis from infected humans and immunised mice
abstract: BACKGROUND: Yersinia pestis (Y. pestis), the bacterial pathogen responsible for plague in humans, remains a public health threat, particularly in light of the recent emergence of antibiotic resistance strains. METHODS: To better understand the immune response against plague and to identify potential targets for immunointervention, we performed an epitope mapping study of the IgG response against a library of peptides representing 18 Y. pestis proteins. The study included sera from 51 individuals who had recovered from plague, 26 uninfected human controls, and 20 sera from mice protected by a live-attenuated vaccine. FINDINGS: Analysis of human sera revealed 32 reactive peptides distributed across eight protein antigens, whereas analysis of mouse sera identified 187 reactive peptides spanning all 18 proteins. Combined analysis of the human and mouse IgG responses to the 32 human-reactive peptides identified 27 B-cell epitopes located within YopD, YopB, LcrV, FyuA, Pla, Ail, Caf1, and PsaA. Of these, one epitope had previously been described as protective and another as immunodominant, whereas the remaining 25 represent immunodominant epitopes identified in this study. INTERPRETATION: Interestingly, IgG antibody responses to selected YopD and YopB peptides were significantly stronger in pneumonic plague than in bubonic plague, suggesting that the distinct clinical manifestations of the disease may be associated with distinct underlying pathophysiological and molecular mechanisms. Our comprehensive mapping of linear IgG epitopes recognised by convalescent human sera, combined with prioritisation based on their predicted neutralising potential, provides a resource for future studies evaluating peptide-based diagnostics, vaccines, and monoclonal antibody therapies against plague. FUNDING: The project was supported by a grant from Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR).

title: Unravelling the biological divergence of CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders with skin involvement: from clinical risk to precision oncology
abstract: CD30+ T cell lymphoproliferative disorders with cutaneous involvement (CD30+ T LPDs) constitute a highly heterogeneous spectrum of diseases that share overlapping histopathologic features. While lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) represents an indolent, self-resolving entity and nodal anaplastic large cell lymphoma (nALCL) with skin involvement is uniformly aggressive, the remaining entities exhibit divergent clinical outcomes, underscoring the need to define the biological drivers of disease heterogeneity.

title: Gut microbial functional associations with subsequent irritable bowel syndrome in a prospective, paediatric case–control study
abstract: Background The infant gut microbiome undergoes rapid maturation that shapes lifelong gastrointestinal health. Although adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) show characteristic microbial and metabolic alterations, it remains unclear whether these differences precede disease onset. Here, microbiome composition and function in infancy were prospectively associated with future IBS development. Methods Stool samples collected from the All Babies in Southeast Sweden (ABIS) cohort at a mean age of 12.4 (±1.5) months, were analysed using a nested case–control design. Cases included future IBS and/or pelvic and abdominal pain, with the average time between age at stool collection and diagnosis being 11.8 (±5.2) years and a mean age at diagnosis of 12.8 (±5.2) years. Microbial composition was profiled with 16S rRNA gene sequencing (n = 396). Data were processed with DADA2, taxonomically assigned using SILVA database, and predicted functionally with PICRUSt2. Descriptive statistics were analysed using χ 2 or Fisher's exact test, global differences with PERMANOVA, differential abundance with ANCOM-BC2, and pathway enrichment with GSEA. Findings Infants with future IBS risk demonstrated microbial divergence, marked by depletion of short-chain fatty acid producers and expansion of facultative and mucosa-disruptive taxa. Inferred functional profiles exhibited reduced fermentative capacity, greater respiratory potential, accelerated degradation of neuroactive aromatic amines, and case-enrichment of cytochrome bc1 complex respiratory unit. Interpretation Gut microbiome dysbiosis in infants with IBS risk is present many years prior to diagnosis and includes early disruptions in fermentation, redox balance, and amine metabolism that potentially compromise epithelial resilience and promote visceral hypersensitivity. Early detection of microbiome dysbiosis suggests probiotic-based interventions.
