Funding Barndiabetesfonden; Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research; Swedish Research Council; Östgöta Brandstodsbolag; Medical Research Council of Southeast Sweden; JDRF-Wallenberg Foundation; Linköping University; Horizon Europe INITIALISE grant.

title: Non-invasive quantification of lower airway antigen-specific antibodies using exhaled breath particles – an observational proof-of-concept study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Advancements in mucosal vaccine development highlight the urgent need for practical methods to assess immune responses in both upper and lower airways. Although nasal sampling is increasingly standardised, a non-invasive technique for directly assessing antigen-specific antibodies in the distal airways has been lacking. METHODS: We used Particles in Exhaled Air (PExA), a non-invasive method capturing aerosolised respiratory tract lining fluid (RTLF) from the distal airways, to quantify antigen-specific IgA and IgG. Antibodies were measured in paired serum, nasal secretions, and PExA samples from 28 healthcare workers during spring 2025, including 18 with RT-qPCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2, influenza A (H1N1), or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. FINDINGS: Antigen-specific IgA and IgG measurements in PExA samples showed low variability (median CVs: spike-IgA 3.7%, H1-IgA 7.2%, RSV pre-F-IgA 5.3%). Strong correlations (Spearman's rho >0.85, p < 0.0001) were observed between PExA and serum IgG, which may be consistent with a systemic contribution to lower-airway IgG levels. In contrast, IgA correlations were more modest, which may reflect local IgA production in the lungs. IgG and IgA correlated between PExA and nasal secretions, while the IgA/IgG ratio was higher in nasal secretions (median 5.0 vs 0.6, p < 0.0001), consistent with expected isotype distribution in upper and lower airways. INTERPRETATION: This study demonstrates the feasibility of non-invasive measurement of antigen-specific antibodies in the lower airways. Our approach proposes a framework for assessing lower-airway immunity and supporting next-generation mucosal vaccine development. FUNDING: This study was funded by the European Research Council, the Swedish Society for Medical Research, and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

title: Potential biomarker candidates for improving diagnosis and disease treatment in adenomyosis
abstract: Adenomyosis remains challenging to diagnose due to its unclear pathogenesis and clinical overlap with conditions such as endometriosis and uterine fibroids. While non-invasive imaging techniques like transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved adenomyosis detection, histopathological examination remains the gold standard. As this typically requires hysterectomy, it limits fertility-preserving diagnostic options. Therefore, the search for potential biomarkers is essential to improve the diagnosis of adenomyosis. This review summarises current evidence on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbiome biomarkers identified using conventional molecular techniques and high-throughput multi-omics approaches in eutopic endometrium, blood, urine, faeces, cervicovaginal lavage and vaginal swab samples with potential clinical applicability, enhancing diagnostic accuracy, and enabling early detection and monitoring. In addition, describing adenomyosis biomarkers may enhance the understanding of adenomyosis pathogenesis and help identify new therapeutic approaches. Although numerous candidate biomarkers have shown promising results (e.g. STEAP1, TOMM20, GLT8D2, and NME5, hsa_circ_008959/hsa-miR-124-3p/SLC15A4 + VAS score, miR-92a-3p or Weissella confusa, and Lactobacillus zeae), the current evidence remains insufficient for their implementation in routine clinical practice owing to the lack of external validation, standardised methodologies, and large multicentre studies.

title: Decoding adenomyosis: integrative insights from genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational analyses
abstract: Adenomyosis is an oestrogen-driven, inflammatory uterine disorder characterised by endometrial glands and stroma in the myometrium resulting in abnormal bleeding, pain, and poor reproductive outcomes. Multiple contributors to its pathogenesis and pathophysiology have been identified over the years using a variety of experimental approaches and technologies, with gaps in integrating these approaches into a comprehensive paradigm of adenomyosis pathobiology. This review provides integrative insights from recent studies focused on genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational approaches. These demonstrate that select genes are causally linked to adenomyosis and that genomic and epigenetic mechanisms promote the enhanced oestrogen and diminished progesterone signalling and associated inflammation that are pathognomonic of the disorder, supported by orthogonal validation including novel 3D in vitro cell models. In addition, advanced computational tools, including AI-driven platforms that integrate multiomics data, reveal promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating disease progression and symptoms and improving fertility and pregnancy success.

title: Integrative analysis of single-cell, bulk RNA-sequencing and biobank-scale genomic data reveals the bidirectional mediation and joint effects between proportion of beta cells and BMI for type 2 diabetes
abstract: Background The pancreas comprises diverse endocrine and exocrine cell types, whose heterogeneity contributes to type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the roles of cell composition changes remain unclear. Methods We integrated six single-cell and four bulk RNA-sequencing datasets to estimate proportions of nine pancreatic cell types (PCP). Logistic regression assessed associations between PCP and T2D. Mediation analyses evaluated bidirectional effects between PCP and body mass index (BMI). Findings were validated using transcriptome-wide association analysis (TWAS) in the UK Biobank (UKB). Proportion of beta cells (PBC) associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined as the overlapping set of genes that showed higher expression in beta cells than in other cell types and differential expression between individuals with T2D and controls. Findings Higher PBC was significantly associated with lower T2D risk (OR = 0.44, P = 1.93 × 10 −5 ), confirmed in UKB (OR = 0.69, P = 2.31 × 10 −36 ). Low PBC and high BMI jointly increased T2D risk in both bulk RNA-sequencing (OR = 22.06, P = 5.27 × 10 −5 ) and UKB (OR = 5.61, P < 1.00 × 10 −300 ) datasets. Bidirectional mediation between PBC and BMI was observed, with mediation proportions of 17.84% ( P = 0.008) and 32.01% ( P = 0.003), respectively, and validated in UKB ( P = 1.11 × 10 −7 and P = 5.30 × 10 −7 ). Eleven PBC associated DEGs (e.g., HADH , PCSK1, and CASR ) were identified. Interpretation The interrelationship between PBC and BMI provides new insights into the link between obesity and pancreatic beta cell biology, while minimally invasive estimation of PBC from genomic data may facilitate population risk stratification and precision prevention of T2D. Funding This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China, Noncommunicable Chronic Diseases-National Science and Technology Major Project, and US National Institutes of Health.

title: A randomised, double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled phase 3 efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity study of an Ad26.RSV.preF/RSV prefusion F-protein vaccine for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus-mediated lower respiratory tract disease in adults aged 60 years and older
